card.hook: Here's a rare thing: a big modern building, a wide river in front of it, and nothing in the way. That's the Ars Electronica Center from across the Danube, and it's an easy win for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on the promenade in front of the Lentos Kunstmuseum on the south bank of the Danube. From there the Ars Electronica Center is about 340 m to the north-west, across the river, so face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the building across the water. Try 0.5x if you want lots of river and sky, but keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't stretch. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) gets you a tighter crop of the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water in the lower third and the building across the middle, and tap the building, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Dusk is a good time, because car and tram light trails pass near the building. In daylight, a calm day gives the clearest reflections on the water.
card.selfie_here: Try the tiered steps and seating of Ars Electronica Square, the plaza on the east side of the Center. Sit on the steps, use the front camera (or 0.5x to fit more building in) and let the glass building sit behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the Nibelungenbrücke sidewalk while you stand on the riverside near the building, so the whole Center sits centred behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: On the bridge sidewalks, stay well clear of cyclists. Photo rules inside the building vary by exhibition, so ask before you take pictures indoors.
card.challenge: Get the horizon dead level and the water in the bottom third, then see if you can spot the building's reflection before anyone walks into your frame.
card.good_to_know: The Ars Electronica Center is the big modern building on the Danube in Linz. The glass facade of the Lentos Kunstmuseum is also often recommended for river reflections. For a different angle, try Nibelungenbrücke for a straight-on, centred view, or Ars-Electronica-Straße for a head-on shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the promenade in front of the Lentos Kunstmuseum on the south bank of the Danube. From there the Ars Electronica Center is about 340 m to the north-west, across the river, so face north-west.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor takes a selfie with the Center directly behind them. The Ars Electronica Square entry is my best fit from a page that names the plaza and its tiered steps, but that page does not call it a photo or selfie spot, so the 'with the building behind' part is my inference. The bridge entry is a viewpoint for photographing the building, not a named selfie position; the visitor's exact standing point is also inferred. Capturing Travel itself advises checking exact tripod spots on the ground, and it says to reconfirm local tripod policies, but it does not state any rule. The only rule-like item I found is that a museum-photography page says flash is often prohibited at museums, which is not specific to this site or to selfie sticks or tripods, so I left rules empty. Lentos Kunstmuseum's opposite-bank promenade is the reliable place to photograph the building, but no page gives it as a selfie spot.

card.hook: Everyone rides the tram up Pöstlingberg to photograph Linz. You're going to do the cheeky thing and photograph the hill itself, with no tram queues in the shot.
card.stand_here: Climb the wooden steps of the Franz-Josef-Warte lookout tower in Freinberg park, then face north. Pöstlingberg sits across the trees in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the whole hill and the green around it. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the church on top closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the hill on one of the upper lines, and let the tree branches frame the edges.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters the hill and the trees. Pick a clear day so the hill stands out from the sky.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the viewing platform beside the basilica at the top of Pöstlingberg, which is the closest spot to a selfie with the church behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold your phone so the church sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand roughly 100 m east of the basilica, facing west, while you stand with the church behind you; it's a photographer's spot rather than a named path, so check it on the map first.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower is in Freinberg park, so check for access rules or opening times before you go.
card.challenge: Find a branch that curls into the corner of your shot and make it your picture frame.
card.good_to_know: Pöstlingberg is Linz's own hill, a 539-metre rise on the left bank of the Danube. The pilgrimage church and a viewing platform sit on top, and the Linz Grottenbahn is up there too. The mountain tramway (line 50, over the Pöstlingbergbahn) runs up from the city centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Climb the wooden steps of the Franz-Josef-Warte lookout tower in Freinberg park, then face north. Pöstlingberg sits across the trees in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a glass building about 130 metres long, parked right on the Danube and busy reflecting the sky all day. That's Lentos, and it does half your photo work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Ernst-Koref-Promenade, right in front of the main glass façade. The museum lies to the north-west of you from here, so face that way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a straight-on shot of the glass front. If the long building won't fit, tap 0.5x. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) is good for the repeated lettering and the reflections.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go in daylight for sky and river reflections, then stay into the evening when the façade lights up. The night lighting is reported to change colour, so every night looks a little different.
card.selfie_here: Try the riverside promenade right beside the glass façade. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x, and tilt up so the building and the sky and river reflections fill the space over your shoulder. The museum's terrace is also recommended for Danube views through the glass, but we can't say whether it's open to everyone.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Nibelungen Bridge to shoot you with the museum behind you, as you look back across the Danube.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is open public space, but the museum itself may have ticket and opening rules, so check the official site before you go. Building work for a new walking and cycling ramp has been reported at the Nibelungenbrücke approach, so check it when you arrive.
card.challenge: Find the spot where both sky and river show up in the glass, then take one shot where your own reflection isn't photobombing.
card.good_to_know: Lentos is Linz's museum of modern art. It opened in May 2003 and was designed by the Zurich firm Weber & Hofer. Its collection grew from works by Klimt, Schiele and Kokoschka, among others.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Ernst-Koref-Promenade, right in front of the main glass façade. The museum lies to the north-west of you from here, so face that way.

The terrace is named by two guides, but neither confirms whether it is open to all visitors or only restaurant guests. Photo rules for the artworks differ by collection and exhibition, and the Airial page says to check on arrival; that is not a selfie-stick rule, so I left it out.

card.hook: Most big concert halls make you crane your neck. The Brucknerhaus does the opposite: it stretches out low and long beside the Danube, with a curved glass front that faces the water. Grass, trees and river all fit in one calm picture.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Donaupark, the riverside park between the Nibelungenbrücke and the railway bridge. The building is to the west of you, so face west with the Danube close by.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole building in. If it won't quite fit, tap 0.5x. For a close-up of the curve of the glass, try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) and hold the phone steady.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line them up with the roof and the base of the glass, so the long horizontal lines stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Evening can look especially striking when the building is lit from inside, so try night mode. Check the weather first, because the glass and the river both reflect the sky.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Anton Bruckner statue next to the concert hall, on the Danube side of the building. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and step back until the hall fits behind your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the 'Strömung' sculpture in the Donaupark with the Brucknerhaus behind you, and ask a passer-by to take your photo from a few steps back.
card.rules_and_safety: Entry to the Brucknerhaus itself depends on events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the roofline dead level on the gridlines, then add a passing boat on the Danube for bonus points.
card.good_to_know: The Brucknerhaus is Linz's concert and congress hall, named after the composer Anton Bruckner. Finnish architects Heikki and Kaija Siren designed it, and it was built between 1969 and 1973. It opened in March 1974 with the Vienna Philharmonic under Herbert von Karajan, and it hosts about 200 performances a year.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Donaupark, the riverside park between the Nibelungenbrücke and the railway bridge. The building is to the west of you, so face west with the Danube close by.

No page states selfie stick or tripod rules. An airial.travel page says drone use may be subject to local regulations, but that is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so I left it out. A Brucknerhaus page says photos are generally allowed during guided tours if they do not disrupt the tour; that is about interior photography, not selfie sticks, so I left it out too. No page mentioned a safety point.

card.hook: Linz's Hauptplatz is a big open square where people criss-cross in front of the buildings, and that gives your photos life without any effort. You can step back, breathe out and fit lots in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand near Hauptplatz, about 150 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. It's about a 2-minute stroll, so try a few spots on the way and take your first wide shot from the edge of the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole width of the square and the buildings around it. Switch to 1x for natural-looking shots and people, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for building fronts and candid shots of people crossing.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building edges up with the vertical lines so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the square is likely to be quieter. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Find the walk-in 'Linz' lettering sculpture on the Hauptplatz, which the city installed mainly as a photo spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the letters fit behind you. Check what's in the background on site, as we can't promise which building lines up.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the Trinity Column (Dreifaltigkeitssäule) and ask a passer-by to step back towards the edge of the square, so the column fits behind you in a wide shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The Hauptplatz has active tram tracks, so keep clear of the rails when you pose. Please also leave a clear passage for everyone else crossing the square.
card.challenge: Grab a 'Hauptplatz trio': one wide shot, one medium shot and one close-up detail, such as paving, a café table or a passer-by.
card.good_to_know: The square is open space, so you can take wide, airy pictures without any special viewpoint. It looks like a public space, but check the official site before you go in case of events or restrictions. Wipe your phone's camera first, because a smudge shows badly on pale buildings and sky.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Hauptplatz, about 150 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. It's about a 2-minute stroll, so try a few spots on the way and take your first wide shot from the edge of the square.

card.hook: Austria's biggest church looks like a stone spike poking out of a sea of rooftops from up here on the Freinberg ridge. It's much harder to get this view from the streets right beside it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Franz-Josefs-Warte on the Freinberg ridge, on the tower's small platforms or in the nearby clearings. Face east, because the New Cathedral (the Mariendom) is across the city in that direction.
card.zoom: Try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone, to bring the cathedral closer because it's a long way off. Use 1x for a wide shot of the city and river with the cathedral as a small part of it, and skip 0.5x, which shrinks it to a speck.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the cathedral, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Golden hour is the one guides recommend. The warm light should look lovely on the tower and the rooftops.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the church behind you, head to the Linzer Domplatz, the square in front of the Mariendom. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and turn your back to the cathedral. No guide names an exact spot, so move around until the tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Domplatz square in front of the cathedral's facade and hand your phone to a passer-by, so they can frame the whole church and its tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The last stretch to the tower is a dirt and gravel path, so wear shoes with good grip. Upper tower levels may be closed. Inside the cathedral, photos for personal use are generally fine, but skip the flash and be considerate of worshippers. Check the official site for entry details before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower in the upper-middle of your frame with the city and river filling the space below, and see if you can keep the horizon dead level using gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The Mariendom is the largest church building in Austria. The first stone was laid in 1862 and it was consecrated in 1924. Its tower is 134.6 m, two metres lower than the south tower of St Stephen's in Vienna, because the originally planned spire was not approved: no building in Austria-Hungary was allowed to be taller.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Franz-Josefs-Warte on the Freinberg ridge, on the tower's small platforms or in the nearby clearings. Face east, because the New Cathedral (the Mariendom) is across the city in that direction.

card.hook: You'll walk up to the Linz Musiktheater and find it's too big to fit on your screen. That's a good problem, because big straight edges and wide surfaces are exactly what phones photograph well.
card.stand_here: Stand near Musiktheater, right at the phone icon on the map, which sits very close to the building. Face the building and tilt your phone up a little.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so everything fits. Then step back as far as is comfortable and try 1x to take in more of the front. For details like a window pattern, an entrance or a reflection, use 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line them up with the building's edges, and the straight lines will look calm and tidy.
card.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to big surfaces than harsh midday sun. After dark, try night mode and rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the sloping staircase that runs from the forecourt down toward the Volksgarten. The glass front rises behind you, so the building stays in the background. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low so the building fits over your shoulder. This spot is our suggestion from the layout, so have a quick look on the spot to check it works.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the Volksgarten across from the glass front while you stand on the stairs, so the steps and the whole building fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: One listing says photography is typically not allowed during performances, and staff can advise on rules in public areas.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up detail, then wait for a few people to walk through the frame to show how big the building is.
card.good_to_know: The Linz Musiktheater is a theatre building in the city of Linz. Its straight lines and wide surfaces keep the shapes clear even in a quick snap. If you want to see inside, check the official site for opening and visiting information before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Musiktheater, right at the phone icon on the map, which sits very close to the building. Face the building and tilt your phone up a little.

card.hook: A little tram glides out of Linz's biggest square and heads straight for a hill, as if that's perfectly normal. It is for this one, and it makes a great photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Hauptplatz, right by the Pöstlingbergbahn stop on the square, and face the tram stop with the historic buildings behind it. The Pöstlingbergbahn line runs off to the north-west from here.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the tram with the square behind it. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the historic buildings, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter tram shot from the edge of the square.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the tram on one of the vertical lines, tap the tram, and if the sky is bright slide it a little darker so the buildings keep their colour.
card.best_time: Check the timetable and arrive when a tram is due, because an empty rail is a sad photo. In summer you might catch the nostalgic open cars, which only run in that season.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, head up to the Pöstlingberg summit. Try the Grottenbahn entrance, which guides single out for its playful details, or the viewing platform next to the basilica with its twin spires behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the landmark over your shoulder. These spots aren't tram-specific, but they're the best-supported options.
card.rules_and_safety: Hauptplatz is an open public square, but tram timetables and tickets can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few frames as the tram rolls in, then pick the one where it sits neatly on a gridline with the rails leading into the picture.
card.good_to_know: The Pöstlingbergbahn opened in 1898 and for over a century ran from a station in Urfahr. In 2009 it was extended to the Hauptplatz and joined to the city tram network. With a maximum gradient of 11.6%, it's the steepest railway of its kind in Austria, so you can tell your friends you photographed a record-breaker.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Hauptplatz, right by the Pöstlingbergbahn stop on the square, and face the tram stop with the historic buildings behind it. The Pöstlingbergbahn line runs off to the north-west from here.

card.hook: A freight ship slides along the Danube, a bridge curves past, and a castle sits on the hill above it all. That's the Linz Castle shot, and it's easier than it looks.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Schlosspark, the green area behind the castle on its west side. Turn east and the castle sits in your frame with the Danube, a bridge and a wooded slope in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the castle with the river and slope around it. Try 0.5x to squeeze in more slope, bridge and water, and 2x or more to pick out the castle walls and the glass wing.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the river on a lower line to keep it level, and use the dark wooded slope in front to add depth.
card.best_time: Go at sunset. The evening light makes the river look warmer.
card.selfie_here: Try the terrace of the modern south wing. It faces out over the city and the Danube, so the castle is behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the castle sit over your shoulder. Or take one on the Schlossberg steps on your way down, so the castle is behind you.
card.ask_someone: Over on the Urfahr riverbank across the Danube (Urfahr Brückenköpfe), hand your phone to a passer-by and pose by the water, so the old town and the castle are in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The castle museum may have its own photo rules, and flash is often not allowed, so check the signs or ask staff. The museum and its terraces may have tickets or seasonal limits, so check the official site first. Don't block paths, entrances or other people while you set up your shot, and keep an eye on traffic.
card.challenge: Wait for a freight ship to glide past, then catch it with the castle above it. Bonus points for a level river.
card.good_to_know: A Roman fort once stood here, and the castle was first mentioned in writing in 799. Emperor Frederick III lived here from 1489 to 1493, and the main block you see today goes back to a rebuilding ordered by Emperor Rudolf II around 1600. The glass-and-steel south wing replaced one lost in the great city fire of 1800 and was finished in 2009.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Schlosspark, the green area behind the castle on its west side. Turn east and the castle sits in your frame with the Danube, a bridge and a wooded slope in front of it.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found states selfie-stick or tripod rules. The castle-behind orientation for both selfie spots is my inference from the viewpoint descriptions, not a page's wording; check on site. The Schlossberg steps and the Urfahr riverbank are named in the sources but no page gives a precise photo position for them. The Urfahr source is a German-language page; its listed GPS for the castle moat is 48.3041, 14.2861, and a Capturing Travel page gives the castle museum as 48.3053907, 14.282341. card.hook: Cars roll across, people wander over, and the Nibelungenbrücke just keeps drawing one big, bold line through your picture. Bridges are show-offs like that, so let it.
card.stand_here: Stand near Nibelungenbrücke, about 120 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-west and the bridge will run across your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and take one wide shot to show the whole setting. Then try 2x for a closer look at the structure. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of sky and surroundings, and keep the bridge in the middle so the edges don't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines in your camera app and set the bridge along one of the horizontal lines, so it looks straight and not tilted.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day gives soft light that suits a bridge. The blue hour after sunset can look great if the bridge is lit. Midday sun makes harder shadows, but it still works if you keep the sky in the frame.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Schlossberg plateau, on the north edge of the Schlossterrasse at Linz Castle. It sits right above the Danube with a central view that includes the bridge. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you need more room, and keep the bridge over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the northern part of the Schlossterrasse, where the bridge is visible across the Danube, and ask the passer-by to step further back along the terrace so the bridge fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Getting up to the castle hill involves stairs and steep paths, so give yourself some extra time. It looks like an ordinary public area, but check local signs before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames while a car or a walker crosses, then pick the one where they land in just the right spot. Bonus points if the bridge stays perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: Nibelungenbrücke is one of the bridges in Linz. It gives you strong lines, a clear shape and plenty of space around it. From the stand-here point it's about a 2-minute walk to the bridge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Nibelungenbrücke, about 120 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-west and the bridge will run across your frame.

card.hook: The outside of the Old Cathedral is pretty plain, and that's exactly why it photographs so well. Two onion-domed towers stand guard either side of the door, and the whole thing is tidy and symmetrical.
card.stand_here: Stand near Domgasse, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the front of the church with both towers ahead of you. Step back a little if you want more sky around them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're close to a big building. Switch to 1x for a calmer view, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one onion dome.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or the lightest part of the wall, then slide it a touch darker so the facade keeps its detail, and turn on gridlines to line the main door up with the centre.
card.best_time: Go when the light is bright but soft and the facade is evenly lit, not half in harsh shadow. On a sunny day, check the sun isn't sitting right behind the towers.
card.selfie_here: Try the Hauptplatz, where the church's front and tower are on the square side. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the church over your shoulder. There's no exact paving spot, so check your screen until both towers show.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working church, so opening times and photo rules inside can vary. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get both onion domes in one shot with the walls dead straight, then take a second shot of just one dome.
card.good_to_know: The Jesuits built this church between 1669 and 1683. It was the cathedral of the Diocese of Linz from 1785 until the new cathedral took over in 1909. Anton Bruckner was organist here from 1856 to 1868, and the Baroque organ he asked to have altered is still inside. The inside is far fancier than the outside, with pink marble columns and a carved wooden pulpit.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Domgasse, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the front of the church with both towers ahead of you. Step back a little if you want more sky around them.

selfie_spots.why: A photo-spot listing places the Old Cathedral's facade and tower on the Hauptplatz side, and Commons has daytime and night photos taken from the square, so a visitor standing there would likely have the church behind them, but no source confirms that as a selfie spot.

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence: none of the pages I found names a selfie spot with the Old Cathedral behind the visitor, or a spot where a passer-by should shoot the visitor with the whole church in frame. The Hauptplatz entry is inferred from listings and photo file names that show the church from the square, so please verify it on site. No ask-someone spot was named. A Commons photo was taken from Linz Castle toward the Old Cathedral, but no page says a visitor should stand there, so I left it out. Do not confuse this with the Mariendom (New Cathedral) on Domplatz, which the search results returned in large numbers. No page gave rules on selfie sticks or tripods. One airial.travel page says photography inside the Old Cathedral is generally allowed without flash, but that is an interior rule and not a selfie rule, so I did not include it.

card.hook: Some spots hand you a ready-made photo, and the Trinity Column is one of them. It's a tall, clear vertical line, so all you have to do is build the shot around it.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, near Hauptplatz. It's about 35 m south of the column, so stand there and face north.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole column in. Drop to 0.5x if you want more of the surroundings, or go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details near the top, so you don't have to walk right up to the base.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the column up with one of the vertical lines, then tap the column and drag the slider to make it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Early morning or early evening is worth a try if you'd like fewer people in the shot. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Look for the big yellow 'Linz' letters on the Hauptplatz. A travel guide shows a visitor posing inside the sign with the Holy Trinity Column behind them. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the column over your shoulder. The sign may be temporary, so check it's there when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at one of the Hauptplatz's corners and shoot back toward the column, which gives a wide frame showing the whole monument.
card.rules_and_safety: The Hauptplatz is mostly pedestrian but has active tram tracks, so stay clear of the rails when you pose or set up a shot. Access to the column couldn't be confirmed, so check locally.
card.challenge: Take three frames: column dead centre, column off to one side, and one with a passer-by walking through to show how tall it is. Pick your favourite later.
card.good_to_know: The Trinity Column is a tall monument in Linz with a strong vertical shape. Pointing your phone upward makes tall things lean inward, so check your photos for converging lines. Stepping back or forward a little changes how much sky and surroundings you get.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, near Hauptplatz. It's about 35 m south of the column, so stand there and face north.

card.hook: Landhaus Linz isn't a big-view stop. It's the kind of place where straight lines and quiet corners do the work, so slow down and enjoy it.
card.stand_here: Stand near Klosterstraße, about 85 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Walk a little way towards the building if you want a closer look at the details.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole building. If you can't fit it in, drop to zoom 0.5x, but keep the building away from the edges of the frame so the lines don't look stretched. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for windows or decoration.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon usually shows the surface of a building best. Midday sun can make the shadows harsh.
card.selfie_here: Head to the official Fotopoint at the Landhaus main entrance (Landhausplatz 1), which was set up to get the Landhaus tower in the frame. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, hold the phone a bit low, and let the tower sit behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the Promenade park path facing the building, with the Hessendenkmal war memorial at the south-west corner of the Promenade in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for access information before you go. The Fotopoint is marked as step-free, but check its exact spot when you arrive.
card.challenge: Find one window, doorway or pattern of light and shade on the wall, and get a shot of it with no people in the frame. Patience counts as skill here.
card.good_to_know: Landhaus Linz suits you if you like architecture more than big views. The city and province installed the Fotopoint at the main entrance. Inside, an arcaded courtyard with the Planet Fountain in the middle is another photo spot, but check access first.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Klosterstraße, about 85 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Walk a little way towards the building if you want a closer look at the details.
